title: Homophones and commonly confused words
blurb: Choose the right word every time between their/there/they're, its/it's, affect/effect, than/then and the other high-yield pairs.
question: An email from a clinic says, “Your going to receive you're results sooner then expected, and the new schedule should not effect you're visit.” How many words are wrong, and how do you test each one?

teach.body: Formally, homophones are words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning (their, there, they're). Commonly confused words are near look-alikes or near sound-alikes (affect, effect; accept, except). Plain English: spell-check cannot save you, because every option is a real word. The TEAS puts the wrong twin into a sentence, so you must decide by meaning and by the job the word does: noun, verb, possessive or contraction.

teach.body: Priya Shah, a nursing applicant, tests each word. “Your going”: expand to “you are going,” which works, so you're. “You're results”: “you are results” breaks, so your. “Sooner then”: it compares, so than. “Effect you're visit”: it follows should and acts as a verb, so affect; and “you are visit” breaks, so your. Five fixes: “You're going to receive your results sooner than expected, and the new schedule should not affect your visit.”

items: If one option has an apostrophe, expand it to two words and reread.
Decide the job: is the blank a noun, a verb, a comparison or a time word?
Match the job to the word: advice (noun) vs advise (verb), than (comparison) vs then (time).
Reread the whole sentence with your choice; every word must fit.

teach.text: The commonest TEAS traps are its/it's, their/there/they're, affect/effect and than/then in context. Watch for options that fix one word but swap a different one: “It's clear the clinic changed it's policy” fixes the first and breaks the second. Every word in the option must be right.

items: Apostrophe = contraction: it's, they're, you're, who's. Possessives have none: its, their, your, whose.
Affect is usually the verb (to influence); effect is usually the noun (a result).
Than compares; then tells time or sequence.
Advice, device and breath are nouns; advise, devise and breathe are verbs.
Decide by the word's job and meaning, then reread the whole sentence.

summary: You can now choose the correct word in the high-yield homophone and look-alike pairs by expanding contractions and identifying each word's job. You can also check every word in an option, so a fix that breaks a different word does not fool you.

A.q: Which sentence uses their, there and they're correctly?
options: Their parking their car over there.
They're parking there car over there.
They're parking their car over their.
They're parking their car over there.
A.why: They're = they are; their shows the car belongs to them; there names a place.

whyNot.0: “Their parking” should be “they are parking”: they're.
whyNot.1: The car belongs to them, so it is their car, not there car.
whyNot.2: “Over there” names a place, so it needs there, not their.

A.q: Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence: “The new medication did not ___ her sleep, and it had no side ___.”
options: effect; affects
affect; effects
affect; affects
effect; effects
A.why: After “did not” the blank needs a verb meaning to influence (affect); after “side” it needs the noun meaning results (effects).

whyNot.0: Both words are swapped: the verb is affect and the noun is effects.
whyNot.2: The second blank is a noun (side effects), not the verb affects.
whyNot.3: The first blank follows “did not,” so it needs the verb affect.

A.q: Which sentence uses than and then correctly?
options: Ana arrived earlier then Ben, and then she checked in.
Ana arrived earlier then Ben, and than she checked in.
Ana arrived earlier than Ben, and then she checked in.
Ana arrived earlier than Ben, and than she checked in.
A.why: “Earlier than Ben” is a comparison (than); “then she checked in” gives the sequence (then).

whyNot.1: Both words are swapped: comparison takes than and sequence takes then.
whyNot.3: “And ___ she checked in” shows what happened next, so it needs then.

B.q: Which sentence uses principal and principle correctly?
options: The principal explained the principle behind the new rule.
The principle explained the principal behind the new rule.
The principal explained the principal behind the new rule.
The principle explained the principle behind the new rule.
B.why: A principal is the head of a school (a person); a principle is a rule or belief.

whyNot.1: Both are swapped: the person is the principal and the rule's idea is the principle.
whyNot.2: The idea behind a rule is a principle, not a principal.
whyNot.3: A person who explains is the principal, not a principle.

B.q: Which sentence uses advice and advise correctly?
options: The nurse will advice you to follow her advise.
The nurse will advise you to follow her advise.
The nurse will advise you to follow her advice.
The nurse will advice you to follow her advice.
B.why: After “will” the sentence needs the verb advise; after “her” it needs the noun advice.

whyNot.0: Both are swapped: the verb is advise and the noun is advice.
whyNot.3: “Will ___ you” needs a verb, so advise.

B.q: Which sentence uses it's and its correctly?
options: It's clear that the clinic changed it's policy.
It's clear that the clinic changed its policy.
Its clear that the clinic changed its policy.
Its clear that the clinic changed it's policy.
B.why: “It is clear” works, so it's; the policy belongs to the clinic, so its.

whyNot.0: “Changed it is policy” breaks, so the second word must be its.
whyNot.2: “It is clear” is meant, so the first word needs the apostrophe: it's.
whyNot.3: Both are swapped: the first is it's and the second is its.

C.q: Which word in this sentence is used incorrectly? “The patient was conscience of the stationary bike in the corner, and the nurse paid her a compliment on her progress.”
options: stationary
compliment
progress
conscience
C.why: Being aware is conscious; conscience is a moral sense.

whyNot.0: A bike that does not move is stationary, so it is correct here.
whyNot.1: A compliment is praise, which is what the nurse gave.
whyNot.2: Progress is used correctly and has no common look-alike in this sentence.

C.q: Which sentence uses loose and lose correctly?
options: If the bandage is too loose, you may lose it.
If the bandage is too lose, you may loose it.
If the bandage is too loose, you may loose it.
If the bandage is too lose, you may lose it.
C.why: Loose means not tight; lose means to misplace.

whyNot.1: Both are swapped: not tight is loose, and misplace is lose.
whyNot.2: “You may ___ it” means misplace, so it needs lose.
whyNot.3: “Too ___” describes the fit, so it needs loose.

C.q: Which sentence uses all of its commonly confused words correctly?
options: The nurses were already to accept every patient except one.
The nurses were all ready to accept every patient except one.
The nurses were all ready to except every patient except one.
The nurses were all ready to accept every patient accept one.
C.why: All ready means completely prepared; accept means receive; except means excluding.

whyNot.0: Already means “by now”; prepared is all ready.
whyNot.2: To receive patients is to accept them, not except them.
whyNot.3: Excluding one patient needs except, not accept.

reteach.title: The apostrophe is a squeezed-out letter
reteach.question: Imagine the apostrophe as a tiny bandage covering a missing letter. When a word wears one, what letters is it hiding?

blocks.body: It's hides the i in “it is.” They're hides the a in “they are.” You're hides the a in “you are.” Who's hides the i in “who is.” So when you see an apostrophe in a pronoun, peel the bandage off and read the full words. If the sentence still makes sense, keep it. If it sounds silly (“the dog wagged it is tail”), the word needs no bandage: its.

blocks.text: For non-apostrophe pairs, ask what job the word does: a thing (advice, breath, effect) or an action (advise, breathe, affect).

explain.body: Expand any apostrophe word into two words. If the sentence still works, keep the contraction; if not, use the possessive (its, their, your, whose).

test.q: Which sentence uses who's and whose correctly?
options: Whose on call tonight, and who's pager is this?
Who's on call tonight, and who's pager is this?
Who's on call tonight, and whose pager is this?
Whose on call tonight, and whose pager is this?
test.why: “Who is on call” works, so who's; the pager belongs to someone, so whose.

whyNot.0: Both are swapped: “who is on call” needs who's, and ownership needs whose.
whyNot.1: “Who is pager” breaks, so ownership needs whose.
whyNot.3: “Who is on call” is meant, so the first word needs who's.

explain.body: To shows direction or starts an infinitive (to stay). Too means also or excessively (too tired). Two is the number. Than compares; then marks time or sequence.

test.q: Which sentence uses to, too and two correctly?
options: The two interns were too tired to stay.
The two interns were to tired to stay.
The two interns were too tired too stay.
The too interns were two tired to stay.
test.why: Two is the number, too means excessively, and to starts the infinitive “to stay.”

whyNot.2: The infinitive is “to stay,” with to.
whyNot.3: The number is two, and excessively is too.

explain.body: In most TEAS sentences, affect is the verb (to influence) and effect is the noun (a result). A noun clue (a, an, the, positive) points to effect; a verb clue (can, will, may) points to affect.

test.q: Which sentence uses the word effect correctly?
options: Caffeine can effect how well you sleep.
The cold weather will effect attendance.
Stress can effect your blood pressure.
The new schedule had a positive effect.
test.why: After “a positive,” the word is a noun meaning result: effect.

whyNot.0: After “can” the word is a verb meaning influence: affect.
whyNot.1: After “will” the word is a verb meaning influence: affect.
whyNot.2: After “can” the word is a verb meaning influence: affect.

explain.body: Several pairs differ only in job: breath, advice and device are nouns; breathe, advise and devise are verbs. Find the job of the blank first, then pick the word.

test.q: Choose the words that correctly complete the sentence: “The nurse told the patient to ___ slowly and hold each ___ for a count of three.”
options: breath; breathe
breathe; breathe
breathe; breath
breath; breath
test.why: “To ___ slowly” needs the verb breathe; “each ___” needs the noun breath.

whyNot.0: Both are swapped: the verb is breathe and the noun is breath.
whyNot.3: “To ___ slowly” needs a verb, so breathe.
